newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin upbeat on Chechnya but aides critical.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin upbeat on Chechnya but aides critical.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin appeared to offer new prospects of greater autonomy for Chechnya on Tuesday, forecasting a political settlement would give the rebel region more "sovereignty" while preserving Russia's borders.

But new strains between Moscow and Grozny quickly came to the fore when one of Yeltsin's top aides accused the separatist Chechen leadership of "hypocrisy" and a television boss with close links to the Kremlin charged them with complicity in the abduction of three of his journalists.
Yeltsin met Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov on Monday for the first time since signing a peace treaty in May to formally end the 1994-96 war.
The two agreed to set up a joint commission to draw up a long-term political settlement defining relations between the mainly Moslem southern province and Moscow.

"This group will create the foundations for bilateral relations," Yeltsin told reporters on Tuesday. "Raising, of course, the level of their (the Chechens') sovereignty, independence, freedom and so on.
"But some areas will remain common ground," he added during a visit to the opening day of the Moscow Air Show.
"A common economic sphere, that already means a single state," he added, saying he also foresaw common defence, military and border defence policies.

Russian news agencies said Yeltsin again cited the example of Tatarstan, a mainly Moslem region in central Russia, which won autonomy but not outright sovereignty in 1994 -- shortly before Yeltsin sent troops to try to crush the Chechen separatist drive.
Maskhadov said after Monday's talks in Moscow he believed Yeltsin would grant Chechnya full sovereignty, saying the president was perhaps the only man able to settle centuries of conflict.
The former guerrilla commander is seen as a moderate in Moscow, which welcomed his election in January.
But Maskhadov has since been under pressure at home from a wave of kidnappings and banditry and because Moscow has been slow to provide funds to rebuild the war-damaged region.
He urged Yeltsin to strike a political settlement soon to restore some stability to the region. Yeltsin, however, made clear on Tuesday he was not to be hurried.
"Let the commission work as long as it has to. Six months, a year. What matters is the outcome," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

On a separate, jarring note, the head of NTV commercial television, who played a leading role in Yeltsin's re-election campaign last year, accused Mashkadov's vice-president of running a hostage-taking racket that the Chechen leader was either too weak to break up or chose to ignore.

At a news conference attended by three NTV journalists who were released on Monday after 100 days in captivity in Chechnya, Igor Malashenko said his group paid a seven-digit sum in dollars to secure their freedom.
"All this is a big hostage-taking machine...under the direct leadership of Vice-President Vakha Arsanov," Malashenko said.

"We are sure that President Maskhadov...is at the very least aware of what is going on...and...is either too weak and cannot help to free people or can and doesn't want to," he added, urging Yeltsin to take steps to stamp it out.
Boris Berezovsky, a deputy secretary of the Kremlin Security Council who negotiated the peace deal, accused Chechen leaders of hypocrisy for claiming credit for freeing the journalists.
Berezovsky was quoted by RIA news agency as saying only the work of Russian special forces and a big ransom had settled the matter.

"Both sides have begun to be hypocritical. I have no doubt that if we go on in this vein, at the end of the day we're going to end up with a severe conflict," he added, stressing Moscow would never agree to Chechnya seceding completely from Russia.
